body:
What is a mural painting?

A mural is a painting executed on a wall, ceiling or another permanent architectural surface. In Indian art history, important murals survive in rock-cut caves, monasteries and temples. Unlike a miniature painting, which is usually made on a relatively small and movable surface such as paper, a mural forms part of the building itself.

Ancient Indian murals are important sources of cultural history. They depict religious stories, royal courts, clothing, ornaments, musicians, dancers and aspects of everyday life. Through these paintings, historians can understand both the religious ideas and the social environment of the period in which the paintings were created.

Mural painting

A painting made on a wall, ceiling or other architectural surface. It may depict a single subject or a connected narrative containing several events.

Murals as a form of storytelling

Many Indian murals are narrative paintings. Instead of showing only one moment, a narrative mural can represent several episodes of the same story within a large painted composition.

A king, prince or another central character may appear more than once, performing different actions in different settings. The repetition does not necessarily indicate several different people. It can represent successive events involving the same character.

This method is particularly useful for understanding the Buddhist Jataka murals of Ajanta, where stories unfold through palace scenes, journeys, encounters and other events.

Religious subjects and their meanings

  • Jataka stories: Accounts of the previous births of the Bodhisattva, the being destined to become the Buddha. They commonly illustrate virtues such as compassion, generosity, wisdom and self-sacrifice.
  • Events from the Buddha's life: Episodes associated with the historical Buddha, including his life and religious teaching. These differ from Jatakas because they concern his final life rather than earlier births.
  • Hindu religious narratives: Episodes associated with Shiva, Vishnu and stories from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Puranic traditions.
  • Jain religious subjects: Depictions associated with Jain religious figures, teachings and narratives.

The subject of a painting is an important identification clue, but it must be considered together with its location and style. A royal court scene, for example, is not necessarily a Hindu painting; it may illustrate a Buddhist Jataka.

How ancient wall paintings were made

At sites such as Ajanta, painters worked on a carefully prepared surface rather than applying colours directly to bare rock. A plaster ground was laid over the rock, and the figures were outlined and coloured.

The Ajanta paintings employed natural pigments and binding materials. The Archaeological Survey of India distinguishes their method from true fresco, in which pigments are applied to wet lime plaster. Ajanta's paintings were executed using a binding agent over a prepared surface.

The general term mural therefore describes the location and nature of the artwork. It does not mean that every mural was made by exactly the same painting technique.

The four principal identification sites

The following four sites illustrate important regional and religious traditions of Indian mural painting:

  • Ajanta, Maharashtra: Buddhist cave murals, especially Jataka narratives and paintings associated with the Buddha.
  • Bagh, Madhya Pradesh: Buddhist monastic murals that also depict royal, courtly and social life.
  • Ellora, Maharashtra: A rock-cut complex associated with Buddhism, Hinduism and Jainism, containing surviving mural fragments as well as extensive sculptures.
  • Lepakshi, Andhra Pradesh: Vijayanagara-period temple murals depicting Hindu religious and epic narratives.

The basic identification rule

Identify a mural through the combination of its subject, artistic style, architectural setting and geographical location. A single clue may be insufficient, but several matching clues usually establish the correct tradition.

Prelims focus

  • A mural is a painting on a wall, ceiling or architectural surface.
  • Jatakas describe the previous births of the Bodhisattva.
  • Ajanta and Ellora are in Maharashtra.
  • Bagh is in Madhya Pradesh.
  • Lepakshi is in Andhra Pradesh.
  • Trap: A royal or dancing scene does not automatically indicate a Hindu subject; Buddhist murals also portray palace life.

[Sources: NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, chapter 'Painting', pp. 105–107; NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, chapter 'Buildings, Paintings and Books', pp. 126 and 129; Archaeological Survey of India, 'Ajanta Caves', section 'Painting Technique' (consulted 23 November 2026).]

title: Understanding Indian Murals: Meaning, Subjects and Identification

body:
Location and historical background

The Ajanta Caves are situated in Maharashtra, in the region historically associated with Aurangabad. The caves were excavated in a horseshoe-shaped rock face overlooking the Waghora stream.

Ajanta developed as an important centre of Buddhist religious life and artistic activity. Its excavations include monasteries, known as viharas, and prayer halls, known as chaityagrihas. The caves contain sculpture and some of the most celebrated surviving paintings of ancient India.

Ajanta's artistic activity extended over several centuries. Its paintings are commonly studied in two broad phases.

The early phase

The earliest surviving paintings are represented by fragments in Caves 9 and 10, associated with the period around the 2nd–1st centuries BCE.

These paintings use comparatively limited colours and sharply defined outlines. Figures are often broad in proportion and arranged in narrative groups. Their appearance shows connections with the early Buddhist sculptural traditions represented at sites such as Sanchi and Bharhut.

The later phase

The most celebrated surviving paintings belong mainly to the 5th–6th centuries CE, when important artistic activity occurred under the Vakatakas and their associates.

Important paintings survive in Caves 1, 2, 16 and 17. This phase is associated with more developed narrative compositions, expressive figures and sophisticated treatment of colour and form.

The Vakataka ruler Harishena belonged to the period of significant activity at Ajanta. His minister Varahadeva dedicated Cave 16 to the Buddhist community, while Cave 17 was associated with the patronage of a local ruling family allied to the Vakatakas.

The patrons who supported cave excavation and decoration should not automatically be identified as the painters. The individual artists responsible for most Ajanta murals are not known by name.

Principal subjects of Ajanta painting

Ajanta paintings are predominantly associated with Buddhism. Their major subjects include:

  • Jataka narratives: Stories illustrating earlier births of the Bodhisattva and the virtues demonstrated in those lives.
  • Episodes from the Buddha's life: Events and teachings associated with the Buddha.
  • Bodhisattva figures: Compassionate spiritual figures represented through elaborate visual imagery.
  • Contemporary social life: Palace interiors, processions, ornaments, garments, musicians, attendants and other aspects of society represented within the paintings.
  • Decorative subjects: Floral and geometric designs, especially on ceilings.

Two important Bodhisattva paintings, Padmapani and Vajrapani, are particularly well preserved in Cave 1. These figures are different from the narrative scenes of the Shibi and Mahajanaka Jatakas, even though they belong to the same broader Buddhist painting tradition.

How to recognise the Ajanta style

The mature Ajanta style is marked by rhythmic outlines, graceful postures, expressive gestures and the modelling of rounded human forms.

Artists used changes in colour and tone to suggest the volume of bodies. Faces often have elongated or partly closed eyes, while the arrangements of figures create a sense of movement and interaction.

Painted architectural features help establish the location of a scene, such as a palace chamber or another setting. The viewer can follow the activities of different characters through a broad composition.

The paintings also provide evidence of contemporary material culture. Jewellery, clothing, elaborate hair arrangements and palace furnishings appear frequently in narrative scenes.

These stylistic features should be considered together rather than treated as absolute rules. The paintings differ across caves and periods, partly because different groups of artists worked at Ajanta.

Why Ajanta is important for mural identification

Ajanta provides a strong association between Buddhist subject matter, rock-cut cave architecture and narrative painting.

When a painting is described as illustrating a previous birth of the Buddha through a succession of palace and other scenes, Ajanta becomes an important possible identification.

The association becomes especially strong when the question mentions Shibi, Mahajanaka, Cave 1 or the celebrated 5th-century paintings.

Prelims focus

  • Ajanta is located in Maharashtra.
  • Its major religious association is Buddhism.
  • Early paintings survive in Caves 9 and 10.
  • Important later paintings survive in Caves 1, 2, 16 and 17.
  • The later painting phase is prominently associated with the Vakatakas.
  • Trap: Padmapani and Vajrapani are Bodhisattva figures; Mahajanaka and Shibi identify Jataka narratives.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art Part-I, Class 11, chapter 'Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture', pp. 37–41; Archaeological Survey of India, 'Ajanta Caves', sections 'Excavation and Architecture', 'Vakataka Period' and 'Paintings of Ajanta' (consulted 23 November 2026).]

title: Ajanta: Buddhist Cave Murals, Narrative Art and Painting Style

body:
Jataka stories as visual narratives

The Jatakas describe earlier lives of the Bodhisattva. In these stories, the future Buddha may appear as a king, prince, animal or another being who demonstrates an important moral quality.

The painted narratives of Shibi and Mahajanaka are important examples of how Ajanta artists represented ethical teachings through memorable human situations.

Both narratives involve kingship, but they emphasise different qualities. Shibi is principally associated with exceptional generosity and self-sacrifice, whereas Mahajanaka is associated with determination, kingship and eventual renunciation of worldly life.

Shibi Jataka: Compassion and self-sacrifice

The Shibi Jataka, also written as Sibi Jataka, concerns a virtuous king who is willing to make an extraordinary personal sacrifice to protect another living being.

The familiar story of the dove and the hawk

In one well-known version, a dove seeks refuge with King Shibi while being pursued by a hawk.

The king promises to protect the frightened bird. The hawk argues that it too needs food and should not be deprived of its prey.

To protect the dove without denying the hawk's need for food, Shibi agrees to offer flesh from his own body equal in weight to the dove.

A balance is brought, and the king places pieces of his flesh upon it. Despite his sacrifice, the dove appears to outweigh the flesh. Eventually, the king offers his entire body.

The test reveals the extraordinary extent of his compassion and generosity.

Shibi identification

King Shibi, dove, hawk, weighing balance and the offer of his own flesh are the decisive elements of the familiar Shibi narrative.

Shibi paintings at Ajanta

The Shibi narrative is represented at Ajanta, including in Caves 1 and 17.

The Cave 1 depiction follows the familiar version involving the hawk, dove and sacrifice of flesh. The Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts distinguishes this from the version associated with Cave 17 and the Jatakamala literary tradition.

In the Jatakamala version, Shibi demonstrates generosity by offering his eyes to a person seeking the gift of sight.

Thus, the central identifying idea is the king's extraordinary self-sacrifice, although the exact episode may differ between literary versions and painted representations.

Do not assume that every Shibi depiction must contain a dove and a weighing balance. Different versions of the story exist. The hawk-and-dove episode is particularly useful for recognising the Cave 1 narrative.

Mahajanaka Jataka: Kingship and renunciation

The Mahajanaka Jataka narrates the experiences of Prince Mahajanaka, who eventually becomes a king but later recognises the limitations of worldly prosperity.

It is represented in the extensive narrative paintings of Ajanta Cave 1.

The principal events of the story

Mahajanaka belongs to the royal family of Mithila. Following a struggle for the throne, his mother leaves the kingdom, and the prince grows up away from his ancestral court.

When he becomes an adult, Mahajanaka attempts to recover his position. During a sea voyage, his ship is wrecked, but he persists in his effort to survive.

He eventually reaches Mithila, becomes its ruler and marries Princess Sivali.

Later, an experience involving mango trees leads him to reflect upon attachment to possessions and worldly pleasures. He decides to renounce royal life.

Queen Sivali attempts to persuade him to remain in the palace, including through elaborate arrangements intended to attract him to courtly pleasures. The king nevertheless remains committed to renunciation.

What the paintings depict

The Mahajanaka narrative contains royal and domestic settings, including the king, queen, attendants, ceremonial activities and a performance by dancers and musicians.

The dance scene associated with Queen Sivali's attempt to dissuade Mahajanaka from renouncing worldly life is a significant visual identification clue.

These scenes illustrate how Ajanta painters combined an ethical Buddhist narrative with detailed observations of royal society and artistic performance.

Mahajanaka identification

Prince Mahajanaka, Mithila, Queen Sivali, royal life, a palace dance and eventual renunciation are the principal identifying elements.

Distinguishing the two narratives

FeatureShibi JatakaMahajanaka Jataka
Central characterKing ShibiPrince and later King Mahajanaka
Main virtueGenerosity and self-sacrificeDetermination and renunciation
Familiar visual clueDove, hawk and sacrifice of fleshKing, Queen Sivali and palace dance
Ajanta associationCaves 1 and 17Cave 1

A painting containing musicians and a royal audience may illustrate the Mahajanaka narrative. A painting concerned with a king protecting a dove at personal cost points instead to the Shibi narrative.

These associations become more reliable when the scene is identified as belonging to the Ajanta cave paintings.

Prelims focus

  • Shibi and Mahajanaka are Jataka narratives associated with Ajanta.
  • Shibi is associated with generosity and self-sacrifice.
  • The familiar Shibi story involves a dove, a hawk and the king's flesh.
  • Shibi depictions are associated with Ajanta Caves 1 and 17.
  • Mahajanaka Jataka is an important narrative in Ajanta Cave 1.
  • Queen Sivali and the palace dance are important Mahajanaka clues.
  • Trap: The dance scene in Mahajanaka is part of a Buddhist narrative, not evidence that the painting belongs to a separate Hindu court-painting tradition.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art Part-I, Class 11, chapter 'Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture', p. 41; Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, 'Some Aspects of Jataka Paintings in Indian and Chinese (Central Asian) Art', discussion of Ajanta Caves 1 and 17 and section 'Sibi Jataka' (consulted 23 November 2026); Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, Jataka Stories, item 046, 'Mahajanaka's Renunciation' (consulted 23 November 2026); Encyclopedia of Buddhist Arts, 'Ajanta Cave 1: King Sibi Jataka' (consulted 23 November 2026).]
